hooks.text: We purposely crashed a spacecraft straight into a fast-moving asteroid.
Could a direct spacecraft impact actually push an asteroid off course?
Scientists hoped to shift an asteroid orbit by just seventy-press seconds.

title: We Crashed a Spacecraft Into an Asteroid on Purpose
description: NASA deliberately crashed the DART spacecraft into the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos, shortening its orbit by thirty-two minutes.

beats.text: We purposely crashed a spacecraft straight into a fast-moving asteroid.
beats.visual: artist's concept of the DART spacecraft impact on Dimorphos, 2022

beats.text: Launched in November 2021, the DART mission targeted Dimorphos, a small moonlet orbiting Didymos seven million miles from Earth.
beats.visual: diagram of the Didymos and Dimorphos asteroid system, 2022

beats.text: Traveling at roughly 14,000 miles per hour, the probe used onboard autonomous navigation to lock onto its target.
beats.visual: DRACO camera final pre-impact image of Dimorphos surface, 2022

beats.text: On September 26, 2022, the impact was photographed by the Italian CubeSat LICIACube alongside Hubble and James Webb.
beats.visual: Hubble Space Telescope view of the DART impact ejecta plume, 2022

beats.text: Scientists originally hoped the violent collision would shorten the moonlet orbit by just 73 seconds.
beats.visual: artist's concept of James Webb Space Telescope observing DART, 2022
queries: James Webb Space Telescope NIRCam DART

beats.text: Instead, massive debris plumes acted like a rocket engine and punched the rock so hard it shortened the orbit by 32 minutes.
beats.visual: LICIACube snapshot of the asteroid ejecta plume, 2022
queries: Light Italian CubeSat for Imaging of Asteroids image

beats.text: That massive planetary defense success proved we can alter the path of a fast-moving asteroid.
beats.visual: ESA Hera mission artist's concept arriving at Didymos, 2026
